::: {.topic-banner}
**The clinical question**

Who is represented in these data, what was measured, and what does a typical—or unusual—patient look like?
:::

::: {.learning-outcomes}
### By the end of this topic

- Distinguish categorical, ordinal, discrete, and continuous variables.
- Choose and interpret appropriate measures of centre and spread.
- Match common plots to the variable and question.
- Recognise skewness, outliers, and the practical importance of distributional shape.
- Explain why reproducible programming is valuable in health-data analysis.
:::

## Variables come before statistics

A number may measure an amount, label a category, or encode an order. That distinction determines what summaries and plots are meaningful.

| Variable type | What it represents | Useful first summary |
|---|---|---|
| Nominal | Unordered categories | Counts and proportions |
| Ordinal | Ordered categories | Counts, proportions, median category |
| Discrete | Countable numerical values | Mean/median and spread |
| Continuous | Measurements on a scale | Mean/SD or median/IQR |

## Centre and spread belong together

The **mean** uses every value and is sensitive to extremes. The **median** is the middle value and is more robust to skewness. The standard deviation describes typical distance from the mean; the interquartile range describes the width of the middle half of observations.

::: {.callout-important}
A centre without a measure of spread hides how similar—or varied—patients are.
:::

## Visualise the distribution

- Use a **bar chart** for counts or proportions of categories.
- Use a **histogram** to see the distribution of one continuous variable.
- Use a **boxplot** to compare median and IQR across groups.
- Use a **violin plot** when the overall shape of each group matters.

For approximately normal data, around 68%, 95%, and 99.7% of values lie within one, two, and three standard deviations of the mean. This is a useful model, not a rule that real clinical measurements must obey.

## R checkpoint

```r
#| eval: false

library(tidyverse)

patient_data |>
  summarise(
    patients = n(),
    mean_pulse = mean(pulse, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_pulse = sd(pulse, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_pulse = median(pulse, na.rm = TRUE),
    iqr_pulse = IQR(pulse, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

patient_data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = pulse)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5) +
  labs(x = "Pulse (beats per minute)", y = "Patients")
```

## Clinical interpretation

::: {.clinical-lens}
**Good reporting:** name the population and variable, give a compatible pair of centre and spread, describe visible skew or unusual values, and avoid labelling a value “abnormal” from distribution alone.
:::

## Lab-book prompts

1. Which variable type is each field in your dataset?
2. Which summary is most honest for the observed shape?
3. What does the visualisation reveal that the summary statistic does not?
